name: Vibravox
description: A dataset of French speech captured with body-conduction audio sensors. It contains audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors and an airborne microphone used as a reference. The corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are included.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poiree, Veronique Zimpfer, Eric Bavu
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poiree, and E. Bavu, "vibravox (revision 071945b)," 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was developed through a rigorous data collection process. The authors designed and implemented a recording protocol, assembled the necessary hardware, and built dedicated software to ensure a controlled and high-quality data acquisition setup. Recordings were made with six sensors worn simultaneously by participants: five body-conduction sensors and one airborne reference microphone. The recording process consisted of four consecutive steps for each participant: speech-clean, where the participant read French Wikipedia sentences for 15 minutes and each utterance generated a new recording; speechless-noisy, where the participant remained silent but could move, swallow, and breathe naturally for 2 minutes 24 seconds while 3D spatialized ambient noise was played; speechless-clean, repeated for 54 seconds in complete silence to record physiological and sensor noises; and speech-noisy, a final 54-second phase with speech recorded under noisy conditions. A total of 200 participants contributed, with 188 retained after post-processing.
rai:dataCollectionType: Experiments, Direct measurement, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of simultaneous 6-channel audio recordings captured by a Zoom F8n field recorder from five body-conduction sensors and one airborne headset microphone at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution. Text read by participants originates from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise data for noisy subsets came largely from AudioSet and from in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The text used for readings was filtered to simplify the dataset by excluding most proper names and removing utterances containing numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, or syntactic errors. Common text normalization operations were applied, such as lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. For noisy-condition experiments, the speechless-noisy subset was dynamically mixed with the speech-clean subset to simulate real-world noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference. The dataset was split by speaker, with 80% of male and female speakers in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel during recording. Post-processing applied three automatic filters to speech-clean utterances to remove obvious deficiencies. Indicators were extracted using the whispertimestamped model to align transcriptions and identify vocalizations. The filters removed samples with phoneme error rate greater than 10%, samples with insufficient SNR defined as Lspeech50 minus Lsilence50 less than or equal to 1.5 dB, and samples failing a sensitivity drift check where Lspeech50 had to exceed the mean silence level for that sensor. Only speech-clean samples passing all three filters were added. All recordings for the other three subsets were added if the participant's corresponding speech-clean subset was not empty. Voice activity detection timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides, and when adjusted boundaries exceeded the original audio, the audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side to remove artifacts such as mouse clicks.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions. Participants read sentences sourced from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice, and the transcriptions were retained for each utterance. From normalized text, corresponding phonetic transcriptions in the International Phonetic Alphabet were generated using the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For words where the phonemizer produced unwanted language switches, a phase of manual phonetic transcription was performed for unrecognized words such as 'algorithme'.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: text phonemizer of the CoML lab; whispertimestamped model
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors analyzed annotation quality during post-processing by computing phoneme error rate as the Levenshtein distance between the phonetic labeled transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output. Samples with PER greater than 10% were discarded to address discrepancies between labeled transcription and actual pronunciation and ensure high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: CoML lab text phonemizer, whispertimestamped model based on Whisper
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The corpus is publicly available online on HuggingFace. A cited dataset revision is "vibravox (revision 071945b)". No updating timeframe, maintainers, or deprecation policy are explicitly stated.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are reported. The paper also notes that the speechless-clean subset can be valuable for tasks such as heart rate tracking and that the dataset includes physiological sounds. Speaker verification is studied as a biometric authentication task using voice.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors hope the release will drive progress in body-conducted speech analysis and support the development of robust communication systems for real-world applications. The paper discusses applications in military operations, industrial settings, access control, intelligence gathering, voice commands, and monitoring vital signs including heart rate. It also notes that rich biometric data such as heart rate and breathing could aid battlefield forensics, revealing emotional states and tracking life signals during critical events.
rai:dataBiases: To increase representativeness and inclusivity, a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants. The dataset was split with balanced male and female speakers across train, validation, and test. The paper also notes that in-ear microphone performance in noisy conditions can be affected by ear canal anatomy and acoustic sealing issues, and that transmission of external noise is influenced by individual variance.
rai:dataLimitations: The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference under noisy conditions. Some data inconsistencies occurred during collection, including mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, and instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. Post-processing excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences. The filters did not catch all issues, for example when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing. The paper also notes that body-conduction sensors have limited bandwidth due to physical constraints, affecting speech intelligibility and downstream tasks, and that one-size-fits-all in-ear designs may not fit all anatomies properly.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, validation, and testing deep learning models for speech enhancement, speech-to-phonemes recognition, and speaker verification. The speech-clean subset contains most of the training data and uses the airborne microphone as reference. The speech-noisy subset is mainly for testing because it lacks a clean reference. The speechless-noisy subset can be mixed with speech-clean for data augmentation to simulate noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference. The speechless-clean subset can be used for tasks such as heart rate tracking, analyzing sensor noise properties, or generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological and sensor-inherent noise.
